summary: For ages 9-10: read, write, order and compare whole numbers to at least 1,000,000 across numerals, number names and expanded form, determining each digit's value. The central skill is reading by three-digit GROUPS (periods) using the comma as a group marker, with special attention to placeholder zeros (403,072; 500,006) and to comparing by scanning from the highest place first. Large numbers should be grounded in real contexts (populations, distances) so magnitudes carry meaning.
misconceptions: Reading digit-by-digit instead of by groups (misreading 403,072).
Dropping or misplacing internal zeros (403,072 → 43,072 or 4,372).
Misplacing the thousands comma so the group boundary and magnitude are wrong.
Ordering by digit count or left-alignment rather than place value.
Saying 'and' in the wrong place / mangling the thousands word.

activities.title: Periods-based number translator to a million
steps: Build a six-column place-value chart split by a comma into a thousands period and a ones period (e.g. 403 | 072), and add a millions column when showing 1,000,000, which needs seven digits.

Enter or read a number and keep three linked forms in sync: the grouped numeral (403,072), the number name ('four hundred and three thousand and seventy-two') and expanded form (400,000 + 3,000 + 70 + 2).
Read the number by chunks, one period at a time, rather than reciting single digits.
Work deliberately on zero-heavy numbers: write 500,006; write 'four hundred thousand and seven' as a numeral (400,007); read 403,072 aloud.
Place each number on a 0-1,000,000 number line and tie it to a real quantity such as a city's population.
activities.insight: A six-digit number is read and built as two three-digit groups; internal zeros are placeholders that hold a column empty, and that empty column still needs its 0 so the magnitude stays correct.

activities.title: Compare and order six-digit numbers from the highest place
steps: Compare pairs such as 548,301 and 543,801, aligning them by place and scanning from the highest place first.
State which single place decides the comparison and stop there (here the thousands digit: 8 > 3, so 548,301 > 543,801).
Order a set of four six-digit numbers from smallest to largest, justifying each step by place value.
Include pairs that differ only in a middle place so the deciding digit is not at either end.
activities.insight: When numbers are aligned by place value (right-aligned), magnitude is decided by the highest place at which two numbers differ, not by left-alignment, the first digit alone, or the final digits. For whole numbers written without leading zeros, a number with more digits is always larger (100,000 > 99,999), and this is the same rule applied to an extra highest place.

activities.title: Expanded form by place value, not face value
steps: Decompose a six-digit number into place-value parts, naming each digit with its place ('7 tens = 70', not '7').
Rebuild the number by adding the parts back and check it matches the original numeral.
Compare a correct expansion (400,000 + 3,000 + 70 + 2) with a face-value error (400,000 + 3,000 + 7 + 2) and explain which digit is wrong and why.
activities.insight: Each digit's contribution equals its face value times its place value; dropping the place multiplier changes the number.

activities.title: Read big numbers aloud in a real context
steps: Hear or read a real large quantity (a city's population, a distance) and read the numeral back aloud by periods.
Then write the numeral you heard, placing any internal zeros as placeholders.
Discuss what the number means at that magnitude using the number line.
activities.insight: Fluent oral reading by groups and accurate written capture of the same number reinforce each other, and real contexts make the magnitude meaningful.

checkQuestion: Watch across forms. 'Read 403,072 aloud, then write it in expanded form. Now compare 548,301 and 543,801 with < or >. Then write “four hundred thousand and seven” as a numeral.' Watch the placeholder zeros and which place the comparison turns on.
checkAnswer: 'Four hundred and three thousand and seventy-two'; 400,000 + 3,000 + 70 + 2; 548,301 > 543,801 (decided at the thousands digit, 8 vs 3); 400,007.
